newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan policeman to lose job over cover-up - reports.
newsitem.headline: Japan policeman to lose job over cover-up - reports.

text.p: A senior police officer in charge of investigating the cult accused of the Tokyo subway gas attack will lose his job after allegations of a cover-up in a related case, media reports said on Monday.

The reports, carried in various leading dailies and on television stations, said the officer would be replaced after failing to report that a policeman who belonged to the cult had confessed to shooting Japan's police chief last year.

The Japanese media said the officer, Security Department Chief Masaru Sakurai of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department, would be relieved of his post on Tuesday over the handling of the reported confession. However, he will stay on the force in another capacity.
"We take it very seriously that public trust of the entire police force has been jeopardised," Kunimatsu said on Monday.

Government officials said last week that a junior police officer who belonged to doomsday cult Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) was being questioned after confessing to the near-fatal shooting of National Police Director-General Takaji Kunimatsu in March last year.
The confession came to light when Japanese media printed an anonymous letter, probably from a police investigator, accusing Tokyo police authorities of a cover-up.
Sakurai currently heads the massive Tokyo police investigation of the sect and the Tokyo subway gas attack on March 20, 1995, which killed 12 and harmed 6,000 people.
Kunimatsu was shot 10 days later as police were conducting a series of raids on sect buildings.

Japanese media have said the junior officer in question confessed in May to the shooting of the National Police Agency (NPA) chief, saying he acted on the orders of senior cult members in order to disrupt police investigations.

But the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department did not pass on the confession to the NPA, the higher authority, because the man had been giving conflicting testimonies and still appeared to be under the sway of the cult, according to media reports.

Kunimatsu did not say the cover-up was the reason for the senior officer's replacement, but said the decision is to show the determination on part of the police to conduct more fair and strict investigations.
Under Japan's law enforcement system, prefectural police forces are in charge of day-to-day operations in their areas while the NPA supervises inter-prefectural activities.

Following media reports of a cover-up, police started searching a downtown Tokyo canal where the policeman is said to have thrown the revolver he used to shoot Kunimatsu. No weapon has yet been found.
Kunimatsu was shot three times by a masked man as he left home in the morning. He survived and resumed his duties after spending three months in hospital.

Police have blamed the sect, led by guru Shoko Asahara, for the subway gas attack as well as a host of other cases including murder, attempted murder and the illegal production of drugs and weapons. Asahara and about 100 of his cult followers are currently on trial.
